14680: To slant means to go at an angle — not perfectly flat like a tabletop, and not perfectly upright like a wall, but somewhere in between, leaning or tilting in a particular direction. Everything else the word does grows from this central idea.

When something slants, it takes a diagonal position or moves diagonally. It leans.

A rooftop doesn't lie flat and it doesn't stand straight up — it goes at a slope. It slants. Heavy rain, pushed by strong wind, doesn't fall straight down anymore — it slants sideways. A ladder leaning against a wall slants. A road going up a hillside slants upward.

You can also cause something to slant. If you hold a flashlight and tilt it so the beam hits the wall at an angle instead of head-on, you are slanting it. A writer who leans their pen so their handwriting tilts to the right is slanting their letters.

The key feeling in the word is this: something that could be straight or level is instead tilted — leaning definitely in one direction. And the word almost always gives you a sense of which direction. Something slants toward something, away from something, downward, upward, or to the left/right.
Meaning 2: The Figurative Meaning — Biasing Information

This is where the word becomes genuinely powerful. Take the physical idea of "tilting in one direction" and apply it not to a physical object but to information, a story, or an argument. That gives you the figurative meaning:

To slant information means to present it in a way that leans toward one particular viewpoint, at the expense of the full, balanced picture.

Imagine a journalist covering a political scandal. If they slant the story, they don't necessarily make things up. Instead, they choose which facts to put in the headline, which facts to bury at the bottom, which words to use, and whose voice to quote more prominently — all in a way that steers the reader toward one conclusion. The story is tilted, just like a roof. It doesn't give you a flat, even, 360-degree view of the truth. It leans.

"The documentary slanted the evidence to make the corporation look guilty." "Every channel seems to slant its political coverage to please its own audience." "She felt the history book slanted the account heavily in favor of the winning side."

Notice what slanting is not: it is not the same as outright lying. A slanted story can contain only true facts. But by selecting, arranging, emphasizing, and framing those facts in a particular way, the writer creates a false impression of balance. The lean is built into the shape of the story, not necessarily into individual false statements.
The Link Between the Two Meanings

The figurative meaning is not random — it is a direct extension of the physical one, and understanding that connection helps you feel the word deeply rather than just memorize it.

A physically slanted surface departs from being level and neutral. A figuratively slanted piece of information also departs from being level and neutral. In both cases, something that should be balanced is instead tilting to one side. The angle in the first case is a spatial angle; the angle in the second case is a perspective angle. But the underlying idea — a departure from straight, a lean toward one direction — is identical.

Slanting can be intentional or unintentional. A propagandist slants information deliberately to manipulate. A genuinely well-meaning writer can also slant a story without realizing it, simply because their own experiences and beliefs shape which facts feel important to them. The word doesn't always carry a judgment about intent — it describes the result: information that leans.

Slanting exists on a spectrum. A report can be very subtly slanted — a slightly charged word here, a conveniently omitted detail there, barely noticeable. Or it can be aggressively slanted, barely resembling a fair account at all. The same is true physically: a gentle downward slope on a path is a slant, and so is a steep incline on a mountain.

The direction of the lean matters. You don't just slant in a vacuum — you slant toward something or away from something. Physically, a roof slants toward the east. Figuratively, a news story slants toward the government's position, or away from the opposition's. The word always implies a destination for the lean.

"The path slants downward toward the river." — something moves or exists at a downward angle.

"The afternoon sunlight slanted through the blinds." — light coming in at a diagonal, not straight in.

"He slanted his eyes toward the window." — he tilted or directed his gaze at an angle.

"The report was slanted in favor of the developers." — the information was biased toward one side.

"She felt the coverage slanted against the protesters." — the information tilted away from giving one group a fair account.

To slant is to tilt — physically, it means to be or move at a diagonal angle; figuratively, it means to tilt the presentation of information so it leans toward one viewpoint rather than giving a straight, balanced account.
14681:
Slapdash describes something done too quickly and too carelessly, resulting in poor quality. When something is slapdash, the person who did it clearly didn't take enough time, didn't pay attention to detail, and didn't bother to check or improve the result.

Think of it this way: imagine a painter hired to paint your walls. A slapdash painter rushes through the job — there are drips on the floor, patches of wall he missed, uneven edges near the ceiling, and streaks everywhere. The job is technically "done," but it is messy, incomplete, and looks terrible. That is slapdash work.
The Two Ideas Packed Into One Word

Slapdash captures two ideas at the same time, and you need both to truly understand it:

1. Speed — the thing was done in a rush, without allowing enough time.
2. Carelessness — the person didn't try hard or pay attention to quality.

These two things feed each other. Because the person rushed, they were careless. Because they were careless, the result suffered. Slapdash is not just "fast" — fast work can still be excellent. And it is not just "lazy in a slow, unbothered way" either. Slapdash is specifically the combination of hurrying through something + not caring about how it turns out.
What Slapdash Work Looks Like in Real Life

Here are the kinds of signs that tell you something was done in a slapdash way:

  • Errors and mistakes that a little extra care would have caught — typos in a document, wrong measurements in a structure, missed steps in a recipe.
  • Incompleteness — parts that were skipped or forgotten because the person was rushing.
  • Unevenness or inconsistency — some parts look fine while others look neglected.
  • A "good enough" attitude — the person stopped as soon as the task was barely finished, without checking or refining anything.

• "His slapdash essay was full of spelling mistakes, repeated points, and a conclusion that had nothing to do with the introduction."
  • "The shelf fell off the wall because of the slapdash way it had been installed — the screws weren't even properly tightened."
  • "She gave a slapdash apology — two sentences, no eye contact, and then she walked away."
  • "The report was so slapdash that her manager sent it straight back and told her to redo it properly."
  • "You could tell the garden had received slapdash care — weeds everywhere, half-dead plants, and a broken fence nobody had bothered to fix."

Notice that in every case, the result is visibly poor — and the reason is clearly a lack of effort and attention, not a lack of skill or resources.
What Slapdash Implies About the Person

When you call someone's work slapdash, you are making a quiet judgment about their attitude, not just the quality of the output. You are implying that they:

  • Did not respect the task enough to take it seriously.
  • Prioritised speed or convenience over doing it properly.
  • Did not care enough about the result — or about the person receiving that result.

This is why slapdash carries a note of criticism and disapproval. It is not a neutral observation. Saying "that was slapdash" is like saying "that simply wasn't good enough, and it didn't have to be this way."

Slapdash is a moderately strong criticism — not the harshest thing you could say about someone's work, but definitely not mild. It goes well beyond "a bit rushed" or "slightly imperfect." It signals that the carelessness was obvious and noticeable, and that the result reflects poorly on the effort put in.
What Can Be Described as Slapdash?

The word is very flexible. It can describe:

  • A piece of work: a slapdash report / a slapdash repair job / a slapdash drawing
  • A method or approach: a slapdash approach to cooking / his slapdash way of doing things
  • An effort or attempt: a slapdash effort / a slapdash attempt at an apology
  • A person (by their habits): She is a slapdash worker — meaning carelessness and rushing are her pattern, not just a one-time thing.

Understanding what slapdash is NOT helps cement the meaning. The opposite of slapdash work is work that is:

  • Meticulous — done with extreme care and attention to every small detail.
  • Thorough — done completely, without skipping anything.
  • Painstaking — done with great effort and patience to get it exactly right.
  • Diligent — done with consistent, careful effort over time.

If slapdash work is a messy, rushed painting full of drips and missed patches, the opposite is a painter who takes their time, uses a steady hand, checks every inch, touches up imperfections, and leaves the walls looking flawless.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Slapdash has a slightly informal, conversational feel to it. You are more likely to hear it in everyday speech, journalism, or casual writing than in very formal academic or legal documents. That said, it is a perfectly respectable word and not rude or vulgar — it simply sounds more natural in ordinary contexts than in, say, a formal business report.
Slapdash means done quickly and carelessly, with too little effort or attention to quality — producing a result that is noticeably messy, incomplete, or full of errors.
14682:
When you describe something as slapstick, you mean it involves a type of humor that is loud, exaggerated, and based on physical actions — things like people falling down, getting hit by objects, bumping into walls, throwing pies at each other's faces, or stumbling over their own feet in ridiculous ways. It is comedy that you see rather than hear, comedy of the body rather than the mind.

A slapstick joke does not make you think. It makes you react — you laugh almost before your brain has caught up, because something absurd and physical just happened in front of you.

There are a few clear hallmarks:

1. Exaggeration
Everything is amplified far beyond real life. A character does not just trip — they fly through the air and crash into a stack of boxes. Someone doesn't just get a small bump on the head — they get hit by a falling anvil and see cartoon stars. The scale of the physical disaster is always larger than reality would allow.

2. Repetition
Slapstick comedy loves repeating the same kind of mishap over and over. A character keeps getting hit by the same door. The same person keeps falling into the same hole. The humor builds because the audience knows what's coming, and yet it keeps happening anyway, which makes it funnier each time.

3. Harmlessness (the "cartoon rule")
Even when things look painful or violent, nobody is ever truly hurt in slapstick. This unspoken rule is crucial. The character gets flattened by a truck, peels themselves off the road, and walks away fine. The audience laughs because they know nothing serious has happened. The moment it felt real and dangerous, it would stop being funny and start being disturbing. Slapstick lives in a world where pain has no consequences.

4. Fast pace
Slapstick scenes move quickly. There is rarely a pause for reflection. One thing goes wrong, then immediately another, then another — a chain reaction of chaos. This speed is part of what creates the laughter.

5. No need for language
A slapstick moment works even if you can't hear the dialogue, or even if the characters are speaking a language you don't understand. The physical action carries all the meaning. This is why classic silent films relied heavily on slapstick — the audience couldn't hear anything, so the comedy had to live entirely in the body.
Everyday Examples to Make It Concrete

Imagine a man carrying a tall stack of boxes. He can't see where he's going. He narrowly misses a lamppost, then a pedestrian, then walks straight into a glass door — and the boxes all tumble onto him. That sequence is slapstick.

Or picture someone slipping on a banana peel. The banana peel is practically the symbol of slapstick humor — a simple, physical, completely avoidable accident that results in a comically dramatic fall.

Classic films and cartoons are full of this:

  • Characters getting bonked on the head with frying pans
  • People running into each other from opposite directions and both flying backward
  • Someone painting a wall and accidentally painting themselves into a corner, or onto another person
  • A ladder swinging around and knocking over everyone nearby
The Register: Is It Highbrow or Lowbrow?

Slapstick is considered lowbrow humor — that is, it is not "sophisticated." It doesn't require any knowledge, cleverness, or cultural background to appreciate. A five-year-old and a seventy-year-old can both laugh at someone falling off a chair, even if they share no language in common. This accessibility is both slapstick's great strength and the reason some people look down on it.

When someone calls a comedy "slapstick," they are often gently signaling that it is not subtle or intellectual humor — it is broad, obvious, and direct. Sometimes this is a mild criticism (implying the comedy is cheap or lazy), and sometimes it is simply a neutral description. Context tells you which one the speaker means.
How It Differs from Other Types of Humor

It helps to understand slapstick by placing it next to other comedic styles:

  • Wit / wordplay relies on clever use of language, puns, or unexpected word choices. Slapstick has nothing to do with words.
  • Satire mocks society, institutions, or human behavior through irony and exaggeration of ideas. Slapstick mocks the body and physical situations, not ideas.
  • Deadpan humor is funny precisely because the comedian delivers absurd things with a completely straight, emotionless face — it is subtle and controlled. Slapstick is the opposite: loud, wild, and visually chaotic.
  • Dark humor finds comedy in genuinely serious, painful, or morbid subjects. Slapstick deliberately avoids genuine pain — it stays firmly in a consequence-free, cartoon world.
How the Word Is Actually Used

"Slapstick" can describe a movie, a scene, a comedian's style, or an entire genre of entertainment:

  • "It was a slapstick comedy — people kept falling off ladders and into buckets of paint."
  • "His humor is very slapstick; he relies on falling down and making funny faces rather than telling clever jokes."
  • "The film has a few slapstick moments, but mostly the comedy is dry and understated."
  • "Children tend to love slapstick humor because physical mishaps are universally funny and require no explanation."

You will also encounter the word used metaphorically, outside of comedy contexts, to mean something that is chaotically disorganized and embarrassingly clumsy — like a situation that has gone so wrong it looks almost comedic:

  • "The meeting was a slapstick disaster — the projector broke, someone tripped over the cables, and the presenter's notes blew out the window."

Here, "slapstick" isn't describing a comedy show; it's describing a real-life event that looked like one because of how spectacularly and physically it fell apart.

If you ever need to quickly check whether something qualifies as slapstick, ask yourself: "Is this funny primarily because of an exaggerated physical accident or mishap, in a world where nobody actually gets hurt?" If yes — that's slapstick.
14683: Slapstick is a style of comedy built entirely on exaggerated, over-the-top physical action — things like wild falls, collisions, pies thrown in faces, people running into walls, getting bonked on the head, slipping on banana peels, or accidentally dumping buckets of water on themselves. The key word is exaggerated: the mishaps are far bigger, clumsier, and more ridiculous than anything that would happen in real life, and they are played purely for laughs.
The word actually has two related meanings

As a noun, "slapstick" refers to two things:

1. The physical prop — A slapstick, in its literal sense, is a simple device made of two flat pieces of wood fastened together at one end. When you hit something with it, it makes a loud, sharp SLAP! sound. Stage performers in old theater used it to fake-hit each other — the audience heard a satisfying smack, but nobody actually got hurt. This prop eventually lent its name to the whole style of comedy it was used in.

2. The genre of comedy — This is the far more common, everyday use of the word. When someone says "that film is full of slapstick," they mean the film relies on exaggerated physical gags to get laughs. Slapstick as a genre is what most people mean when they use the word.

Three qualities define it:

  • Exaggeration: The physical disaster is wildly over the top. Someone doesn't just trip over a step — they somersault through the air, crash through a table, and land in a wedding cake.
  • Fake harmlessness: Despite all the hitting, falling, and crashing, the character appears fine moments later. The pain is theatrical, not real. This is crucial — without it, the audience would feel sympathy or horror instead of laughter. We laugh because we know it doesn't actually hurt.
  • Visual directness: Slapstick humor requires no words, no cultural knowledge, and no intelligence to understand. The body doing something ridiculous is funny entirely on its own. This is why slapstick crosses every language barrier.

Slapstick appears across almost every format in entertainment history:

  • Silent films: Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton are considered the masters. Since there was no sound or dialogue, physical comedy carried their entire films. Chaplin getting tangled in machinery, Keaton hanging off speeding trains — pure slapstick.
  • Television: Mr. Bean is one of the most famous modern examples. Watch him try to change clothes on a beach without anyone seeing him, or eat a trifle he accidentally dropped a steak into. No dialogue needed — the body tells the whole story.
  • Animation: Tom and Jerry and Looney Tunes are almost entirely slapstick. Tom gets an anvil dropped on his head and simply peels himself off the floor, flat as a pancake. The impossibility is part of the joke.
  • Stage and circus: Clowns have used slapstick for centuries — the oversized shoes, the bucket of confetti that looks like water, the endless pratfalls.
  • Modern films and TV: The Home Alone films, Johnny English, The Pink Panther — all built substantially on slapstick gags.

Slapstick is innocent, silly, and light. There is no clever message, no sharp social commentary, no darkness underneath it. It is the most direct form of comedy that exists: something physically absurd happens, and we laugh. A five-year-old and a seventy-year-old in completely different countries, with no shared language, can watch the same slapstick scene and both burst out laughing simultaneously.
How slapstick differs from other types of humor

Understanding what slapstick is not sharpens the picture considerably:

  • Wit and wordplay depend on language and cleverness. "I used to be a banker, but I lost interest." Slapstick needs zero words.
  • Satire uses humor as a vehicle to criticize society, politics, or human behavior. It has an agenda and a point. Slapstick has no such ambition — it just wants you to laugh at someone falling down.
  • Dark humor finds comedy in suffering, death, or taboo subjects, often with an uncomfortable edge. Slapstick is the opposite: the "suffering" is entirely fake, the character is always fine, and there is nothing uncomfortable about it.
  • Dry humor is subtle, deadpan, and understated. Slapstick is loud, obvious, and maximalist. These two sit at opposite ends of the comedy spectrum.

A few things make slapstick so effective:

  • It triggers a kind of relief laughter — something that looked like it could be painful turned out to be fine.
  • Watching someone else be helplessly clumsy makes us feel, just for a moment, smarter and more in control.
  • The exaggeration signals safety: this is not real, you are allowed to laugh.
  • Because it is entirely visual and physical, it bypasses language and intellect and hits something more primal in us.
A quick test to identify slapstick

If you're ever unsure whether something qualifies, ask three questions:

  1. Is the humor driven by exaggerated physical mishaps, not words or ideas?
  2. Is it played for laughs, not for sympathy or shock?
  3. Does the character seem inexplicably unhurt after something that should have been agonizing?

If the answer to all three is yes — you're looking at slapstick.
14684:
To slash means to cut something with a fast, forceful, sweeping stroke — the kind of movement your arm makes when swinging widely through the air. Think of a swordsman swinging a blade across in one powerful motion, or someone hacking through thick jungle plants with a machete. The result is usually a long, deep cut or gash.

What makes "slash" different from just "cut" is the force, speed, and sweeping nature of the action. A surgeon cuts carefully and precisely. A warrior slashes boldly and powerfully.

When used in a physical, literal sense, to slash means to strike or cut through something in that wide, sweeping way.

  • The knight slashed his sword through the air.
  • The attacker slashed the man's arm with a knife.
  • She slashed through the rope in one clean stroke.
  • He slashed at the tall grass with a stick to clear the path.

Notice the word at — you can slash at something even if you don't fully connect with it. The word captures the attempt and the motion, not just the result.

Nature also "slashes" things in this sense:

  • The rain slashed against the windows all night. (Heavy rain hits hard and sweeps across a surface.)
  • The wind slashed across her face. (A sharp, cutting sensation from fast-moving air.)
The Figurative Meaning: Reducing Something Drastically

This is the most common modern use of the word. When someone slashes a number, a price, a budget, or a workforce, it means they cut it down by a large, dramatic amount — swiftly and decisively, just like a blade.

The key idea here is that the reduction is:

  • Big — not a small trim, but a heavy cut
  • Decisive — done quickly and firmly, without hesitation
  • Often sudden — it can surprise people

Examples:

  • The store slashed its prices by 50%. (Reduced them dramatically)
  • The government slashed the education budget. (Cut it severely)
  • The company slashed 3,000 jobs in one day. (Eliminated them suddenly and in large number)
  • The director slashed 20 minutes from the film. (Removed a large chunk)

When you see "prices slashed!" on a sale advertisement, it means prices have been cut down very aggressively — not just a little discount.

To slash can also mean to attack someone or something with very sharp, harsh words — like a critic who tears something apart.

  • The reviewer slashed the novel, calling it boring and poorly written.
  • The politician slashed his opponent's credibility in the debate.

The imagery here is the same: a swift, powerful strike that leaves damage behind.
The Figurative Meaning: Deleting or Removing from Writing/Text

In editing or writing, to slash something means to cut it out completely.

  • The editor slashed three paragraphs from the article.
  • He slashed the unnecessary lines from his essay.

Again, the sense is of bold, decisive removal — not careful trimming.
What Ties All the Meanings Together

Whether you are talking about a sword, rain, prices, jobs, or words in a document, slash always carries the same underlying feeling:

A swift, forceful, sweeping action that cuts through or cuts down something — leaving a significant mark or result behind.

It is never a gentle, careful, or hesitant action. Wherever you see "slash," expect something dramatic, powerful, and significant.

• Literal (physical): To cut with a big, fast, sweeping stroke.
  • Weather/forces: To strike sharply and sweep across a surface.
  • Prices/budgets/numbers: To reduce by a very large amount, quickly.
  • Criticism: To attack harshly with words.
  • Editing/text: To remove a large portion boldly.
One Final Trick to Remember It

Picture a ninja's blade cutting a wide arc through the air. That single image — fast, wide, powerful, leaving a clear mark — is the heart of every use of "slash." Whether it's cutting rope, cutting prices, or cutting words from a page, that same spirit is always there.
14685:
A slat is a thin, flat, narrow strip of hard material — most often wood, but sometimes metal or plastic. It is flat (not round, not hollow), narrow (much narrower than it is long), and rigid. Think of a ruler or a tongue depressor: that general shape — long, flat, and thin — is the essence of a slat.

What sets a slat apart from a "board" or a "plank" is its size and its role. A plank is thick and wide. A slat is slim and narrow. More importantly, a slat is almost never used alone. Slats are found in groups — arranged side by side or in parallel rows — as part of a larger structure.

Picture a standard wooden window shutter. The horizontal strips running across it — each about two inches wide, thin enough to tilt on a small rod — are slats. They are flat, rigid, spaced slightly apart, and stacked in a neat, parallel row. That image is a perfect model of what a slat looks like and how slats behave together.
Where You'll Find Slats in Everyday Life

Window blinds. This is the most familiar example. The horizontal strips in a venetian blind — the ones you twist with a wand to let in more or less light — are slats. Each one pivots slightly, letting you angle them all at once to control the sunlight.

Bed frames. Many bed frames support the mattress not with a solid base but with a series of flat wooden strips laid horizontally across the width of the frame, like a row of parallel bridges. Those strips are slats. Together, they create a surface for the mattress to rest on. If you've ever assembled a bed from a flat pack, you've probably held a bundle of these in your hands.

Park benches and garden furniture. The boards you sit on — those long, flat strips running the length of a bench's seat and backrest — are slats. This is why there are small gaps between the boards. Each strip is a slat; several of them, side by side, form the bench.

Wooden fences. Some fences use individual vertical or horizontal strips spaced slightly apart rather than solid panels. This is called a slatted fence, and each strip is a slat. The gaps between slats let in a little air and light while still providing a barrier.

Crates and pallets. The wooden strips forming the sides of a shipping crate, or the boards of a wooden pallet, are slats.

The common thread in every case: a slat is one thin strip in a series of similar strips, and together those strips form a surface, a structure, or a barrier.
A Visual Way to Remember It

Think of a xylophone. Each bar you strike with a mallet — that flat, narrow, elongated piece — has the exact shape of a slat. Now take that shape, make it out of wood or metal, and imagine it used not to make music but to hold up a mattress, filter light through a window, or form the seat of a bench. That is a slat.

In aviation, a slat refers to a movable panel built into the front edge (the leading edge) of an airplane's wing. During takeoff and landing — when the plane is flying slowly — these panels extend outward and downward from the wing, creating a small gap between themselves and the main wing surface. This reshaped wing can generate more lift at low speeds, which keeps the plane from stalling.

If you've ever looked out of an airplane window during landing and noticed the wing seeming to open up at its front edge — a slim panel sliding forward and dropping, with a visible gap between it and the rest of the wing — you have seen a slat in action. The same word applies because the concept is the same: a flat, narrow panel that is part of a larger surface and that works in relation to it.
An Informal / Slang Sense (Chiefly British and Irish English)

In older or regional British and Irish speech, "slat" is sometimes used informally to mean a person's mental faculty or sanity — usually in expressions like "he hasn't got all his slats", meaning the person is a little dim or not quite right in the head. This is a rare, colloquial use. You are unlikely to encounter it in modern writing or formal speech, but it is worth knowing it exists so you are not puzzled if you come across it.

A slat is a thin, flat, narrow strip — typically wood, metal, or plastic — that is almost always used as one of several identical pieces arranged together to form a surface, a support, or a barrier. You encounter slats in venetian blinds, bed frames, park benches, wooden fences, and crates. In aircraft, slats are wing panels that extend outward at low speeds to improve lift. And in older British and Irish slang, "slats" can refer informally to one's mental faculties.
14686: The word "slate" as a verb has two main meanings that are used in different parts of the English-speaking world. They are so different from each other that knowing only one could genuinely confuse you when you encounter the other. So let's cover both fully, plus one smaller physical meaning.
Meaning 1 — To schedule or plan something (mainly American English)

When something is slated, it means it has been officially planned, scheduled, or set to happen. Think of it as something being "lined up" or "put on the agenda." This form almost always appears as slated, and is almost always paired with either "for" (followed by a time or date) or "to" (followed by a verb).

Examples:

  • The new airport is slated to open next year. (It has been planned/scheduled to open.)
  • The meeting is slated for Thursday afternoon. (It has been set for that time.)
  • She is slated to become the next CEO. (She has been designated/earmarked for that role.)
  • The film was slated for release in December, but got delayed.

Notice that this meaning carries a slight sense of official designation — it's not just a casual plan, but something that has been formally decided or announced. You would use it when an organization, committee, authority, or schedule has put something in place.

A very important nuance: in American English, "slated" can also mean nominated or chosen for a role, position, or honor, even when no specific date is involved:

  • He was slated as the party's candidate for governor.
  • The young scientist was slated to receive the award.

Here, "slated" means she/he has been picked or designated, not just that something is on a calendar.
Meaning 2 — To criticize very harshly (mainly British English)

In British English, to slate someone or something means to attack them with fierce, cutting criticism — in a review, a speech, an article, or in direct conversation. This isn't mild disapproval. When something is "slated," it is torn apart, panned, or thoroughly condemned. The criticism is blunt and often public.

Examples:

  • Critics slated the film. (The critics gave it devastating reviews.)
  • His performance was absolutely slated by the press. (The press attacked it harshly.)
  • She slated the government's new policy in her speech. (She strongly condemned it.)
  • The restaurant was slated online for its poor service.

The tone here is aggressive. If someone "slates" you, they're not gently pointing out flaws — they are going after you hard.

A note on context: Because American and British English use this word so differently, you must always pay attention to who is speaking or writing. An American saying "the plan is slated" means it is scheduled. A British person saying "the plan was slated" might mean it was attacked and torn to pieces.
Meaning 3 — To cover something with slate tiles (literal/physical use)

This is the most direct and literal use. Since slate is a type of natural rock that splits into flat, smooth sheets, "to slate" can mean to cover a surface — usually a roof — with slate tiles. This is used mainly in construction and architecture.

Example:

  • The workers slated the roof of the old farmhouse.

You are unlikely to come across this meaning very often outside of building or trade contexts, but it is worth knowing so you are never caught off guard.
Quick summary of all three meanings

Slate (verb):

  1. (American English) — To officially schedule, plan, or designate something. "The project is slated for next month."
  2. (British English) — To criticize something or someone very harshly and publicly. "The book was slated by every reviewer."
  3. (Literal/physical) — To cover a surface with slate tiles. "They slated the cottage roof."

The most important thing to hold onto is the dialect difference: same word, same grammar, completely opposite emotional weight depending on where the writer or speaker is from. When in doubt, look at the context — is something being planned, or is something being attacked?
14687:
To slather something means to spread or apply it over a surface thickly, generously, and somewhat carelessly — in a way that suggests abundance rather than precision.

If you slather something, you are not being careful or delicate. You are using a lot of whatever you're applying, and you're covering the surface quite heavily.

There are two ideas fused together in this word:

  1. Thickness — the substance goes on in a generous, heavy layer, not a thin film.
  2. Looseness — the action is casual and indulgent, not careful and controlled.

This is what makes "slather" feel different from a plain word like spread. When you spread butter on toast, you could be doing it neatly and sparingly. When you slather butter on toast, there's so much of it that it's practically dripping. There's a sense of "going all out."

The word is typically used with soft, thick, creamy, or sticky substances — things that can be applied to a surface in heavy layers:

  • Food: butter, jam, sauce, cream cheese, mayo, peanut butter, honey, gravy
  • Skin care / body: sunscreen, lotion, moisturizer, sunblock, ointment, aloe vera gel
  • Paint or adhesive: paint, glue, grease, mud
  • Medicine: salve, balm, antiseptic cream

Basically: anything that can be generously smeared, coated, or plastered onto something.

Here are sentences that show it in real use:

  • She slathered peanut butter all over the bread before adding the jam.
    → She put a thick, heavy layer of peanut butter on the bread.
  • He slathered sunscreen on his kids before they ran onto the beach.
    → He applied sunscreen generously and quickly, covering them well.
  • The chef slathered the ribs with barbecue sauce before putting them on the grill.
    → A thick, abundant coat of sauce was applied to the ribs.
  • She slathered on the moisturizer after her shower every morning.
    → She used a lot of moisturizer and applied it freely.
  • The mechanic slathered grease onto the gears to keep them from grinding.
    → He applied grease heavily over the gears.

"Slather" can also be used figuratively (non-literally), usually to mean applying something intangible — like praise, attention, flattery, or affection — in an over-the-top, excessive way.

  • The director slathered the new actor with compliments after the first rehearsal.
    → He praised the actor excessively and in an almost overwhelming way.
  • The advertisement slathered the product with exaggerated claims.
    → The ad coated the product in a heavy layer of excessive, over-the-top claims.

The figurative use keeps the same two key ideas: abundance and lack of restraint.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

"Slather" is not a neutral, clinical word. It carries a sensory, vivid tone — it makes you almost feel the thick substance being applied. It is often used in contexts of:

  • Indulgence (slathering butter on fresh bread feels luxurious and a little excessive)
  • Practicality over elegance (slathering sunscreen on a child is about coverage, not neatness)
  • Enthusiasm (slathering sauce on ribs is done with gusto)

You would not use "slather" in a precise, technical, or delicate situation. A surgeon does not "slather" antiseptic on a wound — that's too casual a word for a careful procedure. A child, however, might slather antiseptic cream on a scrape, putting on more than necessary in a hasty, heavy-handed way.
How It Compares to Similar Words

WordWhat it implies
SpreadNeutral; can be thin or thick, careful or casual
SmearMessy, uneven application; often unintentional or careless
CoatAn even, complete layer; more controlled
DabA small, gentle, light amount
SlatherA thick, generous, indulgent, freely-applied layer

Slather sits at the "heavy and free-handed" end of the scale. It is more enthusiastic than coat, more intentional than smear, and far more generous than dab.

To slather = to apply something in a thick, generous, unhurried layer — covering a surface fully and freely, without worrying about being neat or conservative with the amount.

If you remember one image: a child slathering peanut butter on a piece of bread — piling it on thick, spreading it carelessly, using way more than strictly necessary — that is slather in its purest form.
14688:
A slattern is a woman who is habitually dirty, untidy, and slovenly — in both her personal appearance and her living environment. The word doesn't describe someone who had a messy week or forgot to do laundry. It describes a pattern of behavior, a chronic, ongoing neglect of cleanliness and order. Think of a woman who consistently lives surrounded by clutter and filth, rarely washes, and shows little to no care about her own hygiene or the state of her home.

The key word here is habitually. It's not a bad day. It's a way of life.

This word carries two related but distinct meanings, and both are important to know:

1. The slovenly meaning (the primary one)

This is the most common and widely recognized meaning. A slattern is a woman who is disgracefully and persistently messy, dirty, and unkempt. She might wear stained, disheveled clothes. Her house might be in constant disorder — dishes piled up, floors unwashed, surfaces grimy. She does not take care of herself or her surroundings, and this neglect is not occasional but characteristic of her.

This sense emphasizes physical untidiness and uncleanliness above all else.

2. The morally loose meaning (the older, secondary one)

Historically, the word was also used to refer to a woman considered to be promiscuous or of low moral character — essentially, a woman regarded as sexually loose or disreputable. This meaning is older, less common in modern usage, and you are more likely to encounter it in older literature than in contemporary writing or speech.

In many older texts, these two meanings blurred together, because in historical culture, a woman's physical slovenliness was often associated — unfairly — with moral looseness.
The Tone: This Is a Strong Insult

Make no mistake — slattern is a harsh, contemptuous insult. It is not a gentle or neutral word. When someone calls a woman a slattern, they are looking down on her with scorn and disgust. The word carries deep disapproval and judgment. You would never use it in polite or neutral description.

It is also old-fashioned and archaic. People do not commonly use this word in everyday modern speech. You are far more likely to encounter it when reading 18th- or 19th-century English literature than to hear it in conversation today.
Where You'll Actually Encounter This Word

Because it is archaic, slattern appears most often in classic literature, period dramas, historical fiction, and older texts. Writers like Charles Dickens, Henry Fielding, or authors of that era used the word freely. If you're reading older English novels or plays, knowing this word will help you understand the characters being described and the moral judgments being passed on them.

These are simple, clear examples to help the meaning sink in:

  • "The landlady was a slattern — her apron was filthy, her hair uncombed, and the kitchen floor hadn't seen a mop in months."
  • "The neighbors whispered that she was a slattern who let her children run wild in a house full of rubbish."
  • "In the novel, the young woman feared nothing more than being called a slattern, so she kept her cottage spotlessly clean."

Notice how in each case, the word points to someone whose uncleanliness is not accidental but a defining feature of who she is.

The adjective form of this word is slatternly, meaning characteristic of a slattern — messy, slovenly, or untidy in a habitual way. For example: "She had a slatternly appearance that put visitors off immediately."

To sum it all up simply:

A slattern is a woman who is chronically dirty and untidy — someone whose slovenliness defines her. The word is a strong insult, old-fashioned in modern usage, and most alive in classic literature. It can also, in older usage, carry the suggestion of loose morals. When you see it, you are meant to understand that the writer or speaker holds this woman in contempt for her persistent failure to maintain basic standards of cleanliness and order.
14689:
Slatternly describes someone — or something belonging to someone — that is habitually dirty, messy, and carelessly untidy. The key word here is habitually. It doesn't mean a person is having a bad day or is temporarily disheveled. It means this is their consistent, ongoing way of being. The disorder is a pattern, not an accident.

Think of it as the visual opposite of neat, clean, and put-together — but taken a step further, because the word also implies the person simply doesn't care enough to do anything about it.

The word can be applied to:

A person's appearance — unwashed hair, stained or wrinkled clothing, general scruffiness that suggests a deep indifference to personal hygiene and grooming. "She shuffled to the door in a slatternly dressing gown."

A person's character or habits — someone who is lazy and careless about cleanliness as a way of life. "As a housekeeper, she was entirely slatternly — dust gathered on every surface."

A place or environment — a home, room, or space that reflects the slovenly habits of the person who lives in or manages it. Greasy surfaces, clutter everywhere, things left to decay. "The kitchen had a slatternly air — dishes piled high, the floor unswept."

A person's manner or movement — there is a looseness, a lack of discipline or care in how they carry themselves. "She moved in a slatternly way, as though even standing upright required more effort than she was willing to give."
The Weight and Tone of the Word

This is not a gentle or neutral word. It is a judgmental word — one that carries strong disapproval. When someone uses slatternly, they are not just making an observation; they are passing a verdict on a person's character. The implication is that the person is lazy, undignified, and lacks self-respect.

It sits closer to words like slovenly or sluttish (in the old, now-rare sense of "untidy," not the modern sense) than to softer words like "messy" or "disheveled." If you called someone "messy," it would feel almost affectionate. If you called them slatternly, it would sting — because you're not just describing their appearance; you're making a judgment about who they are.

Quite strong. It implies:

  • The messiness is chronic, not occasional.
  • The person is beyond careless — almost willfully neglectful.
  • There is something morally lacking about their attitude toward cleanliness and order.

It is not the word you'd use for a tired student whose room got messy during exam week. It's the word you'd use for someone whose home is consistently grimy and neglected, and who shows no sign of caring.
How It Differs From Similar Words

• Slovenly — the closest synonym. Means the same thing (habitually untidy and dirty), but is slightly more neutral in tone and can be applied to anyone. Slatternly carries a harsher, more old-fashioned judgment.
  • Unkempt — focuses mainly on appearance (hair, clothes, grooming) and is much milder. It doesn't carry the moral weight of slatternly.
  • Bedraggled — describes someone who looks worn out and messy due to circumstances (rain, exhaustion, a long journey). It is situational and carries no blame, which is very different from slatternly.
  • Dowdy — means unfashionable and dull in dress, but not necessarily dirty. A very well-cleaned person can still look dowdy.
  • Scruffy — informal and relatively mild. More about looking rough around the edges than about deep-seated slovenliness.

The distinction is simple: slatternly is about dirt, disorder, and habitual neglect, with a strong undercurrent of moral judgment. The others either miss the dirt, miss the habit, or miss the judgment.

Historically, slatternly was used almost exclusively to describe women. The base noun form ("slattern") referred specifically to a slovenly woman, and the word carried not just social disapproval but a particular cultural judgment about femininity and domestic responsibility. You'll encounter this gendered usage frequently in older literature — novels from the 18th, 19th, and early 20th centuries especially.

In modern writing, the word can technically describe any person or place, but its old gendered weight still lingers. This is worth knowing because it helps you understand why the word feels so loaded when you encounter it in older texts.

This is not a word you'll hear in everyday conversation. It belongs primarily to:

  • Literary fiction, especially older novels (think Dickens, Hardy, or Victorian-era writing)
  • Formal or elevated writing where precise, evocative description matters
  • Reviews, essays, or criticism where a writer wants to convey a vivid, judgmental image

It's a word that does a great deal of work in a small space. A single use of slatternly tells the reader not just what something looks like, but what kind of person they're dealing with and how the narrator feels about them.

If you had to boil it down to a single sentence: Slatternly means habitually and carelessly dirty and untidy in a way that suggests a deeply ingrained laziness or indifference — and the word always carries a tone of strong disapproval.
